name: Mr Alvarez
visualNotes: A Belizean man in his late fifties who runs the harbour and the boatyard: weathered light-brown skin, a kind, amused squint, salt-and-pepper hair curling from under a navy cap with a gold cord and an anchor badge, a dark moustache over a short grey beard, a red neckerchief, and a light short-sleeved shirt open at the collar (no jacket: the town is hot).
greeting: You came in on that? I have seen coffins with better lines. Sit down before you fall down.
idle: The pier is free to fish. Everything else needs a boat.
Tide waits for nobody, and nobody in this town waits for the tide.

name: Marisol
visualNotes: A Belizean woman in her early forties who runs the tackle shop: tan skin, a thick dark braid over one shoulder, reading glasses pushed up on her head, small silver earrings shaped like fish hooks, and a sleeveless khaki work shirt with pliers clipped to the pocket. A sceptical, knowing half-smile.
greeting: A bamboo rod and a bone hook. I have not seen a rig like that since my grandmother’s. Does it catch?
idle: Match the hook to the fish, not to your hopes.
A lure is a lie you tell with your wrist. Tell it at the right speed.

name: Old Tobias
visualNotes: A Creole Belizean man in his late seventies, sixty years a fisherman: thin and wiry, deeply lined dark-brown skin, short white hair and white stubble, a frayed straw hat pushed back, and a faded short-sleeved shirt open at the neck. A wide, gap-toothed grin. No cap and no full beard: he must look nothing like the man in the reference portrait.
greeting: Sixty years on this water. Ask me where the fish are and I will tell you where they were.
idle: The sea keeps its books. You only ever see one page.
Every fish I lost is bigger now than the day it got away.

name: Delphine
visualNotes: A Garifuna Belizean woman in her fifties who runs the fish market: strong and sturdy, dark-brown skin, hair tied up in a bright patterned head wrap, gold hoop earrings, and a rubber apron over a T-shirt. Brisk and shrewd: one eyebrow raised, a businesslike smile.
greeting: Fresh is money. Big is more money. Protected is none of my business and none of yours.
idle: Check the board. Restaurants pay double when they are desperate.
Smoked keeps, and smoked sells.

name: Dr Imani Reyes
visualNotes: Dr Imani Reyes, a Black Belizean marine biologist in her early thirties: short natural hair, sunglasses pushed up on her head, a sun-faded field shirt with the sleeves rolled, and a pencil behind one ear. Eager and curious, as if about to ask a question.
greeting: You are the one who came in on the raft. I would very much like to know what you saw out there.
idle: Every fish released is a fish that can be counted.
The tide is the moon's handwriting. Learn to read it.

name: Abena Castillo
visualNotes: Abena Castillo, a Black Belizean woman in her sixties who keeps the town's small natural history museum: silver-grey hair in a neat bun, round tortoiseshell glasses, a loose linen blouse and a beaded necklace. Warm and scholarly, with a patient smile.
greeting: A natural history museum with almost no specimens. You can help with that.
idle: One of each kind. The best of each kind, if you can.
Every wing we finish, somebody in town remembers a story.

name: Seu Raimundo
visualNotes: A riverside man of the middle Rio Negro in his sixties, lean and sun-dark, short grey hair, a faded red cap, a sleeveless shirt and a boat-pole over one shoulder, sitting easy on the gunwale of a wooden canoe.
greeting: Belize? By the sea? Then you have never seen water this colour. Sit, sit. Everyone who comes here wants a canoe and a tucunaré.
idle: The river goes up ten metres every year and comes down again. You learn to keep your house on legs.
Low water is for fishing. High water is for waiting, and for tambaqui.

name: Joelma
visualNotes: A Brazilian woman in her thirties who runs the tackle shop and guides anglers: curly dark hair tied back, a sun hat pushed up, a fishing shirt with rolled sleeves, a pair of pliers on her belt and a peacock-bass lure hooked through one buttonhole.
greeting: You want peacock bass. Everyone wants peacock bass. Good: I sell peacock bass lures.
idle: Worms for the little fish, sardinha for the big ones, and noise on top for tucunaré.
Here the sport fish go back in the water. The law says so, and so do I.

name: Seu Bené
visualNotes: An old riverside fisherman in his late seventies, small and wiry, brown skin creased by sun, a few white whiskers, a straw hat with a frayed brim, mending a cast net on his knees.
greeting: Sixty years on this river and it still surprises me. Sit down. Do you eat jaraqui?
idle: The boto takes the fish off your line if you let him. He is cleverer than both of us.
When the beaches come up, the big fish come with them. Wait for the water to drop.

name: Dr Luísa Prado
visualNotes: Dr Luísa Prado, a Brazilian fisheries biologist in her forties, short black hair, glasses pushed up on her head, a field shirt with a research-project patch, a clipboard and a fish-measuring board under one arm.
greeting: You are the angler from the coast. Good. I count fish for a living, and I need people who know how to let them go.
idle: The pirarucu were nearly gone from these lakes. Now the communities count them every year, and there are more.
A cardinal tetra in an aquarium in Tokyo probably came through this town.

name: Dona Socorro
visualNotes: A Brazilian woman in her fifties who runs a stall on the floating market: a broad smile, hair under a bright headscarf, an apron over a flowered dress, a scale hanging beside her and a basket of silver fish.
greeting: Fish? I buy fish. Jaraqui, pescada, tucunaré, whatever you bring. Tetras too, for the aquarium buyers.
idle: The boto comes for the scraps every morning. He thinks the stall is his.
Big catfish sell well. Pirarara, less so: some people say it is bad luck.
